title: Retros That Actually Change How the Team Works
summary: Most retros end with a wall of notes and no next move. How to pick one small experiment, give it an owner, keep it safe to speak up, and check next week that it worked.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The sticky notes are still on the wall when everyone files out. Some are neat, some are scribbled, one has a coffee ring in the corner. The board is honest: too much work in progress, nobody sure who reviews what, product answers arriving late, and a release checklist people only trust after someone reminds them twice. For an hour, the team named the real friction. Now comes the hard part: will anything be different next week?

If you've sat through a few retros where the same complaints come back sprint after sprint, this post is for you. It covers why retros stall, how to turn one complaint into a small experiment, what keeps people honest, and how to check next week that something actually moved.

Feeling better isn't the output

Most retros that go nowhere fail for a boring reason. The meeting produces relief and no next move. Everyone feels lighter for having said it. The notes get grouped, the facilitator thanks the room, and then Monday arrives with the same pressure. After a few rounds the team learns a sad lesson: you can be honest in retro, just don't expect anything to change.

The Scrum Guide is pretty clear about what a retro is for. Its purpose is "to plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness." The team identifies the most helpful changes, the most impactful improvements get addressed as soon as possible, and they may even go into the Sprint Backlog for the next sprint. In other words, the output of a retro is work: something with a place on the board, the same as a feature ticket.

Pick one change and call it an experiment

Esther Derby and Diana Larsen's Agile Retrospectives splits a retro into five phases: set the stage, gather data, generate insights, decide what to do, and close. The second edition (with David Horowitz) has a whole chapter on making change stick, covering action items, experiments, picking a next step and watching for results. In practice, the fourth phase is the one that gets squeezed. The first three are fun and they overrun, then "decide what to do" happens in the last five minutes while people check the time.

Protect that phase, and use it to pick one change. Big retro actions sound mature and then vanish, because nobody can hold them on a busy day:

Vague actionExperiment version
"Improve communication with product.""For two weeks, every story entering development has one named product decision owner and one example of the edge case we're most worried about."
"Review PRs faster.""Before starting new work each morning, review the oldest open PR first. Check the count of PRs older than two days at the next retro."
"Make releases less stressful.""One named owner for the release checklist each week, rotating. They post it in the channel before the release starts."
"Stop overloading QA.""When QA has more than a set number of tickets waiting, we pause pulling new stories and help test instead."

The word "experiment" does real work here. A permanent rule makes people defend their current habits, and the retro starts to feel like a courtroom. A two-week experiment asks for much less: we're not claiming this is the perfect process, only that the current pain is worth trying something different for a sprint. People agree to try things far more easily than they agree to change forever.

People only say the real thing when it's safe

A team can run Start, Stop, Continue or Mad, Sad, Glad and still dodge the truth if speaking plainly feels risky. People need to know that naming a problem won't turn into blame, a performance note or a private complaint about one person.

Plenty of teams open with Norm Kerth's Prime Directive, from his book Project Retrospectives (full text on the Retrospective Wiki): "Regardless of what we discover, we understand and truly believe that everyone did the best job they could, given what they knew at the time, their skills and abilities, the resources available, and the situation at hand." Reading it out loud won't create safety by itself. What helps is when the facilitator acts on it: steer the talk toward the system, the handoff, the queue, the missing signal. When one person's behavior really is part of the story, describe the behavior and the context and leave the verdict out. The same habit is what makes a blameless postmortem work.

Give it an owner and write it down

A retro action without an owner is a wish. The owner doesn't have to fix everything alone. Their job is to keep the experiment visible: check mid-sprint whether it's actually happening, update the note, bring the result to the next retro, and say early when the action needs help or authority they don't have.

Then write it down, because memory is the first thing to go when delivery gets busy. Five lines are enough:

  • The pain we noticed.
  • The experiment we chose.
  • Who owns the follow-up.
  • When we'll look at it again.
  • The signal that tells us whether it worked.

It can live in the team wiki, a pinned message, or the sprint notes. What matters is that the next retro opens with last sprint's commitment on screen instead of a blank wall. If your team already keeps a decision log, put it there.

Measure behavior, and close what didn't work

Keep the measure small and about behavior. Not every improvement needs a dashboard. Sometimes it's whether PRs older than two days dropped from six to two. Sometimes it's whether product questions got answered before implementation started. Sometimes it's whether support handoff notes stopped bouncing back for the same missing field. Feeling better is nice. A changed behavior is what still holds when the next busy week hits.

Closing old actions takes a bit of nerve. If an experiment didn't work, say so without embarrassment. Maybe the owner had no authority. Maybe the signal was wrong. Maybe the pain was real and the action was too indirect. All of that is useful to know. The unhealthy pattern is keeping a dead action on the list because nobody wants to admit it has become decoration.

A retro that changes things often looks less dramatic than people expect. No big workshop moment, no perfect root cause, no speech. Just a team getting a little more specific about its own work: this hurt us, this smaller habit might help, this person keeps it visible, and this signal tells us if it survived a real sprint.

Try at your next retro

  • Open with last retro's experiment and its signal before anyone writes a new sticky note.
  • Reserve the last 15 minutes for deciding what to do, and leave with one experiment.
  • Rewrite that experiment until someone could observe it happening next week.
  • Name an owner and a check-back date, and put the five-line note where the team will see it.
  • Close one old action that never happened, out loud, and say why.

Before everyone leaves the room next time, ask one question: what will someone be able to see next week that shows this meeting mattered? The answer can be small. It just has to be visible.
